query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the identity of the X element governs whether a stable, coherent protective oxide forms during high‐temperature exposure. Specifically, when X is Al or Si, their strong oxide-forming tendencies promote the nucleation and growth of continuous, dense and slow-growing oxide layers (e.g., Al2O3 or silica-rich phases) that adhere well to the alloy substrate. In contrast, when X is Mn, the more volatile and less stable Mn oxides form mixed or porous scales that are prone to cracking or spallation under thermal stress.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys produced as single- or multiphase metallic solid solutions with X chosen as Al, Si, or Mn.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for defined durations (and/or through thermal cycling) to promote in-situ oxide scale formation.
generation.conditions: Isothermal or cyclic oxidation experiments performed at >900 °C in a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment (e.g., air or a defined gas mixture), with all samples processed and polished under identical conditions to ensure comparable starting surfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and phase composition of the surface oxide layer (its continuity, crystallographic coherence and adhesion to the underlying metal) that forms during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Element-specific oxidation kinetics and thermodynamic stability: Al and Si, due to their high affinity for oxygen and lower diffusivity at high temperatures, form slow-growing, dense oxide scales that act as diffusion barriers and minimize stress accumulation. In contrast, Mn tends to form less protective, mixed-valence and porous oxides that do not effectively hinder further oxidation, leading to thermal mismatch and scale spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature exposure, CrFeCoNi alloys with X = Al or Si will develop thin, coherent and adherent oxide layers with minimal cracking, while those with X = Mn will exhibit thicker, cracked or spalled oxide scales. A baseline CrFeCoNi alloy (without an active X element) should form a mixed, less protective oxide layer under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: A control alloy such as CrFeCoNi without the additional reactive element X (or with an inert substitute) is expected to form a less coherent oxide scale that does not effectively protect against further oxidation at >900 °C.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in the metallic solid-solution state and under thermal exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or moderately corrosive atmospheres. Extreme processing variations or additional secondary phase formation may affect the oxide scale characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in oxide thickness, growth rates, and exact interfacial bonding mechanisms remain to be determined. The influence of multiphase microstructures on local oxidation behavior also introduces uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn using identical processing routes to achieve similar solid-solution microstructures. Subject all samples, along with a CrFeCoNi baseline alloy, to controlled isothermal oxidation tests at 950 °C in air (or a defined corrosive gas) for a fixed time period (e.g., 48 hours) and perform thermal cycling to simulate service conditions.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity using SEM and TEM imaging
Phase identification of the oxide layer using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Adhesion and cohesion of the oxide layers via scratch and pull-off tests
Spallation occurrences and surface morphology comparisons
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-containing alloy develops oxide scales with similar continuity, phase composition, adhesion and resistance to spallation as those observed in the Al- and Si-containing alloys (or if the CrFeCoNi baseline exhibits similar protective oxide characteristics), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata

Abstract: AbstractTogether with the thermodynamics and kinetics, the complex microstructure of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exerts a significant influence on the associated oxidation mechanisms in these concentrated solid solutions. To describe the surface oxidation in AlCoCrFeNi HEA, we employed a stochastic cellular automata model that replicates the mesoscale structures that form. The model benefits from diffusion coefficients of the principal elements through the native oxides predicted by using molecular simulations. Through our examination of the oxidation behavior as a function of the alloy composition, we corroborated that the oxide scale growth is a function of the complex chemistry and resultant microstructures. The effect of heat treatment on these alloys is also simulated by using reconstructed experimental micrographs. When they are in a single-crystal structure, no segregation is noted for α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, which are the primary scale-forming oxides.
